1.pericope_label: The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD... A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the opening clause as the counsels of the heart belonging to man, and denies at the fourth verse that the words teach a decree of reprobation: God created no one for punishment or predestined him to destruction, and the wicked are only made subservient to his purposes, as Pharaoh by rebelling could not alter God's plans but only gave occasion to display his power. He allows the human sense of mercy and truth at the sixth verse, but only as evidence of the faith that works by love, and draws from the second verse the practical rule that a clean conscience is no excuse, so a man should examine himself anxiously and still pray against the faults he has not noticed. Delitzsch corrects three grammarians who took the first verse of a favourable hearing, the point being that a man does not always find the fitting expression for what he has in mind; rejects three ancient versions which read reveal for roll at the third verse; removes the ground of the reprobation question by repointing the fourth so that God made everything for its own contemplated end; takes the mercy and truth of the sixth for love and faithfulness between men; and at the ninth collects the same proverb in German, Arabic and Latin.

Gill reads the first verse of a man who can neither think nor speak without God, picturing the marshalling of ordinarily confused thoughts like an army drawn up for battle; takes the self-satisfied man of the second verse for the self-righteous, ignorant of his own impurity and of the spirituality of the law; presses the literal sense of rolling one's works upon the Lord; and denies at the sixth verse that alms deeds or fair dealing can purge sin, referring the mercy and truth to God.

Clarke puts the second reading of the first verse sharply, the counsels being the free offspring of the heart of man and the answer the free volition of God; reports the Chaldee at the fourth verse, which turns the first clause toward those who obey God; and is the most emphatic of all on the sixth, that the Hebrew is not ambiguous and says He shall atone for iniquity, God by his mercy in sending his Son and the truth of what he promised through the prophets, so that the verse must not be read as though a man could atone by his own charity. Wesley reads the first verse of men unable to think or speak wisely without divine assistance, states the fourth as a sequence rather than a decree — men make themselves wicked and God therefore makes them miserable — and takes the mercy and truth of the sixth as a qualification for offering acceptable prayer for pardon.

Henry gives both readings of the first verse and prefers the second, that man purposes while the answer of the tongue is of the Lord. He generalises the second verse, since we are all partial in judging ourselves, and sets against it the unerring balance in which God weighs the spirits; keeps the received sense of the fourth, making God first cause and last end and noting that the wicked fight him with the very powers he gave them; and instances Esau made to be at peace with Jacob.

debates.question: Does the fourth verse teach a decree of reprobation?

positions.view: No: the words do not mean God created anyone for punishment or predestined him to destruction, only that the wicked are made subservient to his purposes.
The question does not arise on the right pointing, which gives not for himself but for its own contemplated end.
Not addressed directly; the Chaldee turns the first clause toward those who obey God.
God is first cause and last end, and the aggravation is that the wicked fight him with the powers he gave them.
A sequence rather than a decree: men make themselves wicked, and God therefore makes them miserable.

debates.question: Whose mercy and truth expiate iniquity at the sixth verse?

positions.view: God's, and the Hebrew is not ambiguous: He shall atone for iniquity, by his mercy in sending his Son and the truth of what he promised.
A man's own, but only as evidence of the faith that works by love, since such qualities purge nothing in themselves.
A man's own, as qualifying him to offer acceptable prayer for pardon.
Neither: the phrase means love and faithfulness in the relations of men to one another, not the grace and truth of God.
God's in promising and performing, and ours as the condition of the pardon rather than its purchase.

outliers.note: Adds a conjecture of his own at the fourth verse, that since the root literally signifies to feed, the clause might be read of God feeding the wicked daily rather than reserving them for an evil day.
Notes that the first three proverbs of the chapter are absent from the Greek version, their place taken by three others which he judges a compensation only in appearance and not in worth.

themes: The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the Lord.
All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the Lord weigheth the spirits.
Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.
The Lord hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil.
Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished.
By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the Lord men depart from evil.
When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.
Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.
A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the Lord directeth his steps.

10.pericope_label: A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment... In the light of the king’s countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the tenth verse should not transgress, the king being God's representative on earth and dignified by that title in the Psalter, and hears in it an echo of Solomon's youth; on the twelfth and thirteenth he is blunt that what is described is the ideal king, whom Israel's history shows Solomon and the best of his successors fulfilling only feebly, the conception being too high for man and answered only in David's Son; and he explains the latter rain as falling at the end of March to mature the barley and wheat before the April harvest. Delitzsch reaches the same result at the tenth verse by grammar, treating the first line as a noun clause and correcting Jerome and Luther, whose renderings make the proverb assert what it only requires; and at the fourteenth he says the plural strengthens the figure and gives it a face, the wrinkled brow and flaming eye standing for the troop of messengers.

Gill notes that the word behind the divine sentence means divination, and that since the discernment Solomon showed between the two harlots is not found in kings generally, the verse states what ought to be rather than what is. On the eleventh he takes the just weight as of God's devising and appointing; he records that kings in fact hearken to those who flatter their pride and love of power; he takes the messengers of death for the Targum's angels of death and instances the wrath of Ahasuerus falling on Haman; and he turns the light of the countenance toward the King of kings, whose favour and gracious presence are life to his people.

Clarke stands apart at the tenth verse, reading it as a statement of fact about a righteous king: though divination itself were brought to bear on his lips to make him punish the innocent and spare the guilty, they would not transgress, so firmly is he attached to God. On the eleventh he thinks the allusion is probably to the standard weights kept in the sanctuary, though others take it of the weights merchants carried in their girdles — a possibility he supports by observing that the Chinese take no coin but gold and silver by weight and carry a small steelyard for it. Of the twelfth and thirteenth he remarks only that these sayings concern monarchical government rightly administered. Wesley says only that the favour of the fifteenth verse is as acceptable as the clouds which bring the latter rain.

Henry treats the tenth verse as a prayer as much as a proposition: we wish it were always true, and ought to make it our petition for kings and all in authority, but since it is often otherwise the words may be taken as a precept to kings and judges. He makes both halves of the eleventh divine appointments, public justice being an ordinance of God and justice in trade likewise, since he taught men the discretion to make scales and weights at all; treats the good king as a character offered for his successors' instruction rather than a portrait; and on the last two verses adds a political aside of his own, blessing God for a constitution which maintains the prerogative of the prince without injury to the liberty of the subject.

debates.question: Does the tenth verse state a fact about kings or a duty?

positions.view: A duty: such discernment is not found in kings generally, so the verse says what ought to be, not what is.
A duty, and a prayer: we wish it were always true, but since it is often otherwise it may be read as a precept to kings and judges.
A duty, rendered should not transgress, the king being God's representative on earth.
A duty by grammar: the first line is a noun clause, and Jerome and Luther make the proverb assert what it only requires.
A fact about the righteous king, whose lips would not transgress even if divination were brought to bear on them to pervert his judgment.

debates.question: Is the ideal king of the twelfth and thirteenth verses ever realised?

positions.view: No: Israel's history shows how feebly Solomon and the best of his successors fulfilled it, the conception being too high for man and answered only in David's Son.
It is a character rather than a portrait, offered not for Solomon's own praise but for his successors' instruction.
The contrary is the usual case, kings hearkening to those who flatter their pride and love of power.
Not a question worth raising: these are plain sayings about monarchical government rightly administered.

outliers.note: Supports one reading of the weights in the bag with a contemporary observation from China, where no coin but gold and silver by weight was taken and a small steelyard was carried for the purpose.
Breaks off from the eastern kings whose will was law to bless God for the constitution he lives under, which maintains the prerogative of the prince without injury to the liberty of the subject.

themes: A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment.
A just weight and balance are the Lord’s: all the weights of the bag are his work.
It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness.
Righteous lips are the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right.
The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it.
In the light of the king’s countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain.

16.pericope_label: How much better is it to get wisdom than gold!... Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets the sixteenth verse at the head of a series on wisdom, righteousness, humility and trust in God read as a succession of steps, humility being the virtue of virtues and trust in God the condition of all salvation, and notes that such a possession comes by acquisition and not inheritance; he makes the highway one straight and unimpeded road, made so by the avoidance of the evil that would entice a man aside; at the eighteenth he collects a Latin proverb that great things fall, inflated things burst and swollen things are crushed, together with a Hebrew play on two accent names in which a rising is followed by a breaking, insisting that the noun means the fracture of a body rather than bursting or shipwreck; and at the nineteenth he defends the written form of the word against the marginal one, since it may be understood of sufferers as well as of the humble. Ellicott calls the highway the plain way of duty which cannot be mistaken whatever a man's other difficulties, and notes the contrast between pride and the blessing promised to humility just before.

Gill takes the wisdom of the sixteenth verse for Christ, the fountain in whom the treasures are hid; names the highway the King's highway, the way of holiness in which men, though fools, shall not err; supplies the instances of pride's fall from the angels that fell and our first parents down to Haman and Nebuchadnezzar; and puts the humble among the followers of the meek and lowly Jesus, with mean thoughts of themselves and resigned to God.

Clarke sets one question against the whole commendation of wisdom over gold — whether anyone believes it, though it was spoken by the wisest of men under divine inspiration; puts the seventeenth verse in a single clause, that the upright man is ever departing from evil and by keeping that road preserves his soul; and at the eighteenth offers two personifications, pride walking with destruction in its train and haughtiness marching on with ruin behind, before recording the Masoretic note printed in most Hebrew Bibles that this is the middle of the book. Wesley alone allows departure from the highway, calling it the common road of the upright though through frailty they slip into the bypath of sin.

Henry notes how the preference of wisdom over gold is stated — urged with admiration at the disproportion and with an appeal to the reader's conscience — and grounds the difference in giver and beneficiary alike, grace being of God's peculiar favour where gold is of common providence. He makes the highway a public road marked out by authority and tracked by many who went before; presses the certainty of pride's fall, since men cannot punish pride but only admire or fear it, so God takes the punishing into his own hands, and adds that proud men are often most insolent just before their destruction; and calls the last verse a paradox the children of this world will not subscribe to.

debates.question: What kind of road is the highway of the upright?

positions.view: A public road marked out by authority, tracked by many who went before and shared with company met on the way.
A single road, straight and unimpeded, made so precisely by the avoidance of evil enticing aside to right or left.
The plain way of duty lying in front of a man, which cannot be mistaken whatever his other difficulties.
The King's highway, the way of holiness in which men, though fools, shall not err.
Their common road, from which through frailty or temptation they may still slip into the bypath of sin.
Not a road so much as a habit: the upright man is ever departing from evil, and by keeping that road preserves his soul.

debates.question: What is the alternative offered in the nineteenth verse?

positions.view: Two tempers: it is better to be poor and humble than rich and proud, a paradox the children of this world will not subscribe to.
Two companies: on the written form of the word, which needs no correction, it is dwelling lowly among sufferers that is set against dividing spoil among the proud.
Two characters: the humble are the followers of the meek and lowly Jesus, resigned to God and safer from falling than the proud.

outliers.note: Records the Masoretic note printed in most Hebrew Bibles at the eighteenth verse, that this is the middle of the book of Proverbs — the middle verse, whose first clause ends the middle of its words.
Answers the commendation of wisdom above gold with a single sceptical question, whether anyone actually believes it, though spoken by the wisest of men under divine inspiration.

themes: How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!
The highway of the upright is to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud.

20.pericope_label: He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good... He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the object of the twentieth verse to be the divine word, setting the clause against the despising of the word earlier in the book and making attention to it the way to true prosperity; describes the sweetness of the lips in Cicero's phrase for beauty of speech, of no significance for learning itself but of great value for teaching it; corrects two commentators who took the instruction of fools for the teaching fools give, laying down that when fools are the subject the word always means the training given them; defines the pleasant words as words love suggests and that breathe love, the healing promised not only restoring soundness but preserving and advancing it; and reads the labourer's hunger as the thing that labours for him. Ellicott agrees that the twentieth verse concerns attention to God's word, says the power to express thought in graceful language adds greatly to learning's value, sets out both senses of the instruction of fools without deciding, and renders the last verse of the group as the hunger of the labourer labouring for him.

Gill accepts our version at the last verse while remarking that a man who labours to grow rich lays up more for others than himself; and applies the pleasant words to the doctrines of the Gospel, where a Jewish commentator had applied them to the law. He takes the repetition of the warning about the way that seems right as itself the point, the observation being important enough to demand attention twice.

Clarke sees in the wellspring of life another of the book's anatomical allusions, to the artery carrying blood from the heart to the extremities; notes of the honeycomb that honey in the comb is sweeter and finer than what has been pressed out and exposed to air; observes that the warning about the way that seems right is precisely the same as an earlier verse; and states the last verse bluntly, that no thanks are due a man for his industry, since if he does not work he must starve. Wesley keeps the practical sense of the twentieth verse, of a man who orders his affairs with discretion, and puts the gain of eloquence plainly, that a man improves himself while teaching others.

Henry keeps the practical sense of the twentieth verse but adds that prudence only gains repute, and that a man who handles matters wisely while leaning on his own understanding finds little satisfaction in the good he gets. He treats the twenty-third verse as a correction of the twenty-first: Solomon had commended eloquence and seemed to set it above wisdom, but now shows that unless there is a treasure within to support it, it is worth little, and that however fine the language, what is unseasonable had better be unsaid. He takes the rejected sense of the instruction of fools, that nothing good is to be got from a fool whose set discourses are themselves folly; and reads the labouring soul of the last verse as heart-work, since the mouth's continual craving means a man must either work or starve.

debates.question: What is handled or attended to in the twentieth verse?

positions.view: The divine word: giving heed to it is the way to true prosperity, and the clause answers the despising of the word earlier in the book.
A man's affairs: he that is master of his trade and considerate in his business will find good, though prudence alone gains only repute.

debates.question: Whose instruction is folly in the twenty-second verse?

positions.view: The training given to fools; when fools are the subject the word always bears that sense, and two commentators erred in taking it otherwise.
Either — the discipline fools administer is worse than useless, or the discipline they endure is folly, since those who will not be taught by wisdom are corrected by their own foolishness.
The teaching fools give: nothing good is to be got from a fool, whose set and solemn discourses are themselves folly.

outliers.note: Reads the wellspring of life anatomically, as another of the book's allusions to the artery carrying blood from the heart out to the extremities of the body.

Reports that the ancient Syriac took the last verse of the group in an entirely different direction, of a man who inflicts woe suffering it himself, a rendering the Targum brought nearer the text and Luther abbreviated.

themes: He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he.
The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning.
Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools is folly.
The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips.
Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him.

27.pericope_label: An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire... The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD

schools.summary: Delitzsch names the whisperer from a root meaning to murmur; insists that the violent man's enticement is not moral seduction but enticement to a place which makes the intended violence practicable, the noun for violence meaning the injustice of club-law, of a man who puts his own force in the place of God; offers at the thirtieth verse what he calls a warning in physiognomy, biting the lips being the act of the deceitful and the tense implying that a man seen doing it has the evil as good as done; holds length of days to be on one side a natural consequence and on another a promised recompense; and notes that the law ordains the lot nowhere, knowing only one ordeal, its use resting on a parallel custom. Ellicott corrects the conditional of the thirty-first verse to a statement, the crown being found in the way of righteousness because long life is itself promised as the reward of obedience; says victory over self is the hardest of victories; and draws from the lot the encouragement that much we attribute to chance is due to the providence of God.

Gill takes the first of the evil men for a man of Belial, without a yoke, who digs for sin as for treasure and need not go far, having enough in his own heart, and supplies two instances of the practice from church history. He adds a second sense to the shutting of the eyes, that such a man shuts them against the light of Scripture lest his practices be reproved; and allows the use of the lot while hedging it about — never in trivial cases, nor for curiosity or gain, nor rashly, but seriously and religiously, with prayer and in faith.

Clarke compares the digging of evil to quarrying, a wicked man working as hard at an evil purpose as a quarryman at stones, and explains the burning lips as words igniting strife as fire does dry stubble; reads the shut eyes as concentration; is fullest on the man slow to anger, observing that it is easier to subdue an enemy without than one within and that many kings who conquered nations were slaves to their own passions, Alexander among them; and will not say how far the lot is proper now, granting it was once lawful and efficient and is still allowed even by writers on civil law, but adding that those who most need recourse to it are those with neither piety to pray nor faith to trust God for an answer. Wesley reads the shut eyes with Clarke as the gesture of one whose thoughts are deeply engaged, and refers the burning lips to a tongue set on fire of hell.

Henry sorts the evil men of these verses into two kinds, those who envy a man his good name and dig up evil to blast it, and those who like Satan work by force as roaring lions rather than by fraud as subtle serpents. On the hoary head he urges that it ought to be the great care of old people to be found in the way of righteousness, since God and man will look for them there; and on the lot he states the governing principle, that nothing comes to pass by chance and that what man has neither eye nor hand in, God is concerned in, so that such appeals must eye God by prayer.

debates.question: Is the crown of the hoary head conditional on righteousness?

positions.view: Yes, and the condition is the point: it ought to be the great care of old people to be found in the way of righteousness, since God and man will look for them there.
No: the clause is a statement, not a condition — the crown is found in the way of righteousness because long life is itself promised as the reward of obedience.
Both at once: length of days is on one side a natural consequence of such a course and on another its promised recompense.

debates.question: May the lot still be used?

positions.view: Uncertain: it was once lawful and efficient, since the decision was taken as coming immediately from the Lord, and it is still allowed even by writers on civil law — but those who most need recourse to it have neither piety to pray nor faith to trust God for an answer.
Yes, but hedged: never in trivial cases, nor for curiosity or gain, nor rashly or superstitiously, but seriously and religiously, with prayer and in faith.
Yes, when the matter cannot otherwise be decided, and then God must be eyed in it by prayer.
The law ordains it nowhere, knowing only one ordeal; its use rests on a custom running parallel to the law, in private life and public justice alike.
The practical question is left aside for the doctrinal one: much that we attribute to chance is due to the providence of God, and that should encourage trust.

outliers.note: Illustrates the man slow to anger with Alexander, who conquered the world and yet in a fit of intemperate anger killed Clytus, the closest of his friends, and adds that most nations have coined a similar proverb, quoting one from Horace.
Illustrates the digging up of evil from church controversy rather than from Scripture, naming one party that raked up an early father's youthful sins and another that served Beza the same way.

themes: An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire.
A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.
A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good.
He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.
